title: Online Life: Choose What Happens Next
summary: Three situations about a group chat, late-night scrolling and a stranger who asks for a photo. The teen chooses, sees what might happen, and the psychologist leads the discussion.
clinicianNotes: Original scenarios and conversation starters. The third scenario touches on online grooming: follow child-protection and disclosure procedures if the teen reveals a real situation. Draft content: needs review by a licensed psychologist and a cultural fit check before use with patients.

scenarios.title: The group chat
scenarios.story: Someone shares an embarrassing photo of a classmate in the class group chat and people are laughing. Everyone is waiting to see what you will do.

options.text: Do not join in, message the classmate privately to check on them, and tell a trusted adult if it continues.
options.outcome: The laughing slows down. The classmate thanks you quietly and feels less alone.
options.note: Protects the person and uses adult support. Explore what made it possible and what could make it hard.

options.outcome: Nothing changes in the chat, and you feel uneasy about it later.
options.note: Silence is common when the group is loud. Explore the fear of becoming the next target.

options.text: Add a laughing reaction like everyone else.
options.outcome: The chat gets louder, and you feel bad when you picture being in that photo.
options.note: Joining in often protects belonging. Explore what the teen needed in that moment.

scenarios.keyMessage: You can stand up for someone without a big scene. A private message and a trusted adult both help.
scenarios.discussion: What is one thing you could do next time a group laughs at someone?

scenarios.title: One more video
scenarios.story: It is midnight and you have school tomorrow. The next video starts playing and you feel your eyes getting heavy, but you want to keep going.

options.text: Put the phone on charge across the room and tell yourself you can watch more tomorrow.
options.outcome: It is hard for a minute, then you fall asleep and wake up less tired.
options.note: Uses a simple environmental trick. Explore what helps the teen stick to it.

options.text: Watch ten more minutes, then ten more, then fall asleep late.
options.outcome: You get through tomorrow, but you feel foggy and short-tempered.
options.note: The pull of autoplay is designed to be strong. Explore what the teen is escaping or enjoying.

options.text: Keep scrolling until very late and worry about tomorrow when it comes.
options.outcome: You are exhausted at school and slip behind on homework.
options.note: Look for stress or loneliness behind long late-night use. Explore what the teen finds at night that they miss by day.

scenarios.keyMessage: Rest powers mood, memory and friendships. Small tricks beat willpower alone.
scenarios.discussion: Where could your phone sleep tonight so it is easier to rest?

scenarios.title: The friendly stranger
scenarios.story: Someone you only know online keeps messaging you privately. They praise you a lot, ask you to send a photo, and tell you to keep the chat a secret.

options.text: Send nothing, stop replying, block them, and tell a parent or teacher.
options.outcome: You feel nervous, but the adult helps you report the account and you feel safer.
options.note: Clear safe response. Explore any discomfort about telling an adult and reinforce that the teen did nothing wrong.

options.text: Reply politely without sending a photo, and keep it to yourself.
options.outcome: The messages continue and you feel uneasy but unsure what to do.
options.note: Partial protection. Explore secrecy, flattery and why telling feels hard.

options.text: Send the photo because they seem friendly and promised to keep it secret.
options.outcome: Soon they ask for more and threaten to share it, and you feel trapped.
options.note: Follow child-protection procedures if this reflects a real situation. Respond without blame and explore who the teen can tell.

scenarios.keyMessage: Anyone who asks you to keep a secret about private photos is not a safe friend. Telling a trusted adult is always right.
scenarios.discussion: Who are two adults you would feel able to tell if something online made you uncomfortable?
